narrative:
The model estimated an 83.6% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, meaning it judged failure much more likely than success. Because your law school application was tied to that prediction, the application was denied. This is a risk estimate, not a guarantee; it still implies roughly a one-in-six chance of passing. Your gender and race were not used in this prediction.

The denial was driven mainly by your academic standing in law school. Your Year 3 class standing was the single most influential factor: you were placed in the lowest decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile. That gap pushed the prediction strongly toward bar failure. Your Year 1 standing was the second most influential factor, and it showed the same pattern—lowest decile versus an accepted-student average near the sixth decile—adding further risk. Your upper-middle family income was the third most important factor, but its influence was smaller and pointed in the opposite direction, slightly favoring a pass; it was not enough to offset the academic concerns.

To improve your position, focus on the areas the prediction identifies as risks. Strengthen your academic record through additional coursework or a structured bar-preparation program, and consider retaking the LSAT after serious preparation if the schools you target consider it. Seek admissions advising, apply to programs that review candidates holistically, and reapply once you can show improved performance.
